newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: U.N. sees exports vital for former east Germany.
newsitem.headline: U.N. sees exports vital for former east Germany.

text.p: United Nations analysts said on Monday the German government was facing a major regional development problem in the former East Germany where growth this year looked set to lag well behind the west.

In its annual Survey of regional economies, the U.N.'s Economic Commission for Europe (ECE) said it was crucial for the net export performance of the eastern "lander", under communist rule, until 1989 to be improved.
Overall reconstruction of the area "has turned out to be a much more difficult task than generally expected when German economic and monetary union started in July 1990," the Survey said.
The east German economy had seen a radical transformation, and there had been a significant improvement in real incomes of the population, supported by fiscal transfer payments.
But, the Survey added, the overall productivity gap between east and west Germany was still very largeand there were major structural problems which continued to restrain economic growth.

After buoyant economic progress with annual growth rates of 8-10 per cent in 1992-94 reminiscent of the dynamic "tiger economies" of Asia giving hope of rapid convergence, growth in the east had slowed to only two per cent last year.
On current forecasts, real GDP in 1997 would rise by only one per cent compared with two per cent in the west.
"If these forecasts prove correct, this will be the first year in which the process of economic convergence underway since 1991 would be partly reversed," the ECE said.

This would be a metter of concern for German policy-makers given that convergence between the two parts of the country was far from complete, with GDP per head in 1996 in the east still only 54 per cent of the western level.

The Survey said the earlier growth process in the east was largely driven by expansion of the non-tradeable sector -- construction and local services -- which are not exposed to international competition.
Construction had attained a disproportionately large size in the region's economy, accounting for some 18 per cent of growth in 1995 compared with only five per cent in the west.
But the construction boom in the former East Germany peaked in 1996 and a major downsizing of the sector now lay ahead "with negative implications for the labour market," the ECE said.
"The crucial issue now is whether the tradeable sector, and especially the manufacturing industry, can take over as the main engine of growth.

"It is only via a stronger export base that the east German region will be able to prosper and that the need for large net transfer payments can be reduced and ultimately eliminated," the the Survey declared.
